chunks: Ali ibn al-Husayn narrated to us via this chain, from Muhammad ibn Ali al-Kufi, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Hashim, from Abu Khadija, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) that he said:

Indeed, Ali (peace be upon him) said: 'I had the right to kill the fleeing one and finish off the wounded, but I left that for the end-times from among my companions; if they were wounded, they would not be killed. But the Qa'im (peace be upon him) has the right to kill the fleeing one and finish off the wounded.'

key_terms.لِلْعَاقِبَةِ: For the end-times / the later era
key_terms.يُجَهِّزَ: To finish off / to ensure death

ai.seo_question: Why did Imam Ali not kill the fleeing enemy at Siffin and how does it relate to the Qa'im?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Kitab al-Ghayba* highlights the jurisprudential principle of *al-‘Adl* (justice) versus *al-Maslaha* (public interest), where Imam Ali’s restraint at Siffin was a strategic mercy to preserve the dignity of his army rather than a permanent legal prohibition. It establishes a unique eschatological distinction for the Qa'im, who possesses the absolute authority to execute the fleeing (*al-Mawli*) and finish the wounded (*al-Jarih*) as a definitive act of divine justice, contrasting with the temporary political prudence of the early Imams. This underscores the Shia view that the Mahdi’s rule will restore the pure application of Sharia without the constraints of political expediency.

en.abdullah-al-shahin: (15) Ali bin al-Husayn narrated from Muhammad bin Ali al-Kufi from Abdurrahman bin Abu Hashim from Abu Khadeeja from Abu Abdullah as-Sadiq (as) that

Amirul Mo’mineen (as) had said: “I could have killed the fleers and finished off the wounded (warriors) but I did not do fearing for the end of my companions that if they might be wounded, they would not be killed. But al-Qa’im (as) is permitted to kill the fleers and to finish off the wounded.”
